opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think about it a lot. If you look at where AI has had the biggest impact, it's images, text, and audio. In those domains we learned how to go from raw signals straight to predictions. Nobody hand-engineers edge detectors anymore. The model learns the representation end to end.

Structured data is different. Most of the world's valuable data, at companies, hospitals, and governments, doesn't sit in one flat table. It lives in relational databases with many tables: customers, transactions, products, events, all linked by primary and foreign keys. To build a model today, a data scientist has to flatten all of that into one feature table. They write joins and aggregations, things like "number of purchases in the last 30 days" or "average order value." That feature engineering is manual and slow. It's also lossy, because you throw away much of the relational structure and fine-grained temporal signal. Honestly, it looks a lot like computer vision before deep learning, when people hand-crafted features.

So the core issue has been the lack of the right architecture and the right way to represent the data. For images we have convolutions, and for text we have sequences and transformers. For relational data, the key insight for us was that a database is really a graph. Each row is a node, and the foreign-key relationships are edges. Once you see it that way, you can use graph neural networks and graph transformers to learn directly over the raw multi-table data. Information propagates across tables, and the model learns its own features rather than relying on ones a human guessed. That's what we've been calling relational deep learning.

There are other reasons too. Tabular data is very heterogeneous. Every company's schema is different, columns have different types and meanings, and the data changes over time, so you have to be careful about temporal leakage. Also, there was no ImageNet for relational data. That's part of why we built benchmarks like RelBench, so the community could compare methods on realistic multi-table prediction tasks.

The exciting part is that we're now seeing the pieces come together. With these architectures you can even build foundation models for relational data. These are pretrained models that take a new database and a prediction task and give accurate predictions through in-context learning, without months of feature engineering and model building. So I'd say structured data hasn't been transformed yet not because it's less important. If anything, it's the most commercially valuable data there is. We simply hadn't found the right way to let deep learning consume it natively. I think that's changing now.

r001.rationale: The response says current workflows flatten relational data into a feature table and rely on manual feature engineering, but it does not state that changes in model families have left that paradigm fundamentally unchanged.

r002.rationale: It says that in images and text, models learned to go from raw signals directly to predictions and learn representations end to end.

r003.rationale: It contrasts end-to-end learning from raw signals in images and text with structured-data workflows that flatten relational data and require manual feature engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's actually one I think about a lot. If you look at where the value in the enterprise actually sits, it's overwhelmingly in structured data. It's in the data warehouse, in Snowflake, in Databricks, in these relational databases with dozens or hundreds of tables. That's where the customers are, where the transactions are, where the products are. And yet, if you look at where the deep learning revolution has happened, it's been images, text, audio, video, and structured data has largely been left behind.

And I think there are a couple of reasons for that. The first is that, historically, the way we've done machine learning on tabular data is through feature engineering. A data scientist looks at the business problem, say churn prediction, and then they spend weeks or months hand-crafting features. How many times did this customer log in during the last thirty days? What's their average purchase amount? How many support tickets did they open? They flatten all of these tables down into one big table, one row per customer, and then they train XGBoost or a random forest on top of it. And that works, but it's incredibly manual, it's brittle, and it doesn't scale. Every new problem starts basically from scratch.

What made computer vision and NLP work was that we stopped hand-designing features. In vision, we went from SIFT and HOG to convolutional networks that learn the features directly from pixels. In language, we went from bag-of-words to transformers that learn representations directly from raw text. The model learns what matters. And nobody had really figured out the analogous move for relational data. What is the raw input? It's not a single table. It's many tables, connected by primary and foreign keys, with timestamps, with different column types, numerical, categorical, text, time. It's a much messier, more heterogeneous object than a grid of pixels or a sequence of tokens.

The second reason, I'd say, is that the community hasn't had the right abstraction. We've treated a table as a matrix, and if you treat a table as a matrix, you throw away all the relational structure, all the links between entities. And that structure is exactly where the signal is. So our observation, which really comes out of a decade of work on graph neural networks, is that a relational database is naturally a graph. Every row is a node, every foreign key is an edge, and now you can apply message passing directly over this structure and learn the representations end to end, without a human having to decide which features to compute.

And the third piece, honestly, is just that there wasn't the data and the benchmarks. For vision you had ImageNet, for language you had the web. For relational data, every company's schema is different, the data is proprietary, and so there was no shared playground for the research community. That's part of why we put together things like RelBench, to give people a common set of problems so the field can actually make progress and measure it.

So I don't think it's that the problem is unsolvable. I think it's that it was structurally harder, the incentives in the research community pointed elsewhere, and the right building blocks, graph learning, transformers, foundation-model-style pretraining, have only recently come together. And now I think we're at the point where you can genuinely talk about a foundation model for structured data, something that you point at a database and it just predicts, the same way you point an LLM at text. I think that's going to be a really big shift.

r001.rationale: The response says tabular ML still relies on manually engineered features, flattened into one table for models such as XGBoost or random forests, while deep learning transformed other modalities.

r002.rationale: It identifies learning features directly from raw pixels in vision and raw text in language as the shift that enabled progress.

r003.rationale: It explicitly contrasts manual feature engineering and single-table modeling for structured data with vision and language models that learn representations from raw inputs.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that tabular data doesn’t have the same universal structure that images or language have. With images, you have pixels, and the same kinds of visual patterns show up across many different tasks. With language, you have words and sequences. That gives you a shared representation where you can train a model broadly and then reuse what it has learned.

With tabular data, every table can be its own world. One column might represent a customer’s age, another a transaction amount, another an internal product code. Across organizations, those columns have different meanings and different relationships. So it’s much harder to define a common learning problem that lets knowledge transfer from one dataset to another.

And often the data isn’t actually in one table. It’s in a relational database, spread across customers, transactions, products, and so on. A lot of the useful signal is in how those records connect. Traditionally, a data scientist has to turn those relationships into features before a model can use them. That’s a substantial amount of manual work, and it has to be repeated for each prediction task.

So I think the opportunity is to move beyond treating a table as an isolated matrix and build models that can learn directly from the structure and relationships in the data. That could remove much of the feature engineering that makes these applications so difficult to develop today.

r002.rationale: It describes shared representations for images and language, but does not identify learning directly from raw data as the breakthrough that transformed those fields.

r003.rationale: It states that tabular work requires manual feature engineering, but does not clearly contrast this with computer vision and language models learning directly from raw data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that tabular data doesn’t have the same shared structure that images or language have. With images, you always have pixels, and the patterns you learn in one set of images can be useful in another. With language, you have a common vocabulary and a sequential structure. That makes it possible to pretrain a model on a huge amount of data and then apply it to many different tasks.

With tables, every dataset has its own schema. A column means something different from one database to another, and even the relationships between columns are specific to that application. So it’s much harder to define a universal representation that allows knowledge to transfer.

And in practice, enterprise data is rarely just one table. It’s many tables connected through relationships: customers make purchases, purchases contain products, products come from suppliers. When we flatten all of that into a single table for machine learning, we lose structure and spend a lot of effort manually constructing features. I think the opportunity is to learn directly from that relational structure, so the model can use the connections in the data rather than requiring a person to encode them all in advance.
